key_insight: A concise set of design principles — data diversity, strong vision–language alignment, explicit action grounding, and evaluation across realistic tasks/environments — determines whether vision–language–action models become useful generalist robot controllers.
problem_solved: Clarifies which components and trade‑offs matter when building and evaluating vision–language–action models, reducing ambiguity about where to invest effort (data, alignment, architecture, or benchmarks).
method: Systematic comparison of existing vision–language–action model families across task suites and environments.
Controlled analyses (e.g., ablations) to isolate effects of dataset scale/diversity, multimodal alignment strategies, and action-conditioning designs.
Proposal/use of standardized evaluation metrics and benchmarks to assess transfer, robustness, and real‑world task success.
impact: Provides practitioners clear priorities for building generalist robot models—guiding dataset collection, alignment methods, and evaluation choices—so development focuses on factors that most improve real‑world robotic performance.
visual_elements: Block diagram showing the pipeline: Vision encoder → Language encoder → Alignment module → Action policy (with icons for each modality).
Bar chart or radar plot comparing relative importance of factors (data diversity, alignment, action grounding, architecture, evaluation) derived from ablations.
Grid of benchmark tasks/environments illustrating transfer and robustness tests (simulated vs real, tabletop vs mobile manipulation).
Icon set for quick takeaways: dataset, alignment (link icon), policy/robot arm, evaluation/checklist.
paper_title: What matters in building vision–language–action models for generalist robots
paper_authors: Xinghang Li, Peiyan Li, Long Qian, Minghuan Liu, Dong Wang
